title: India and NAM: Phases and Current Role

cards.h: The idea India gave the world
cards.b:
Non-alignment is the best-known idea in Indian foreign policy. It means not joining a military bloc, keeping freedom to judge issues on merit, and working for peace and decolonisation.

The Non-Aligned Movement (NAM) began at Belgrade in 1961 and grew into a group of about 120 states. India was its founder. Today the question is whether non-alignment is still relevant, or whether it has become strategic autonomy and multi-alignment.

UPSC asks about phases, India's changing role and the relevance of NAM after the Cold War. This lesson follows those three themes.

Nehru said India would not join either camp in the Cold War, but it would take a stand on issues. This is different from neutrality (staying out of conflicts) and from isolationism.

  • Independence of judgement: India voted differently on different issues.
  • No military pacts: India refused to join SEATO or CENTO (US-led) and signed no alliance with the USSR.
  • Peace and disarmament: India supported the UN, a nuclear test ban, and cooperative security.
  • Anti-colonialism and anti-racism: support to freedom movements and a stand against apartheid.
  • Economic independence: self-reliance and aid from both blocs.

The 1954 Panchsheel principles (mutual respect for sovereignty, non-aggression, non-interference, equality and peaceful coexistence) guided the policy.

The Belgrade summit (September 1961) had 25 members. The five founders were Nehru (India), Tito (Yugoslavia), Nasser (Egypt), Sukarno (Indonesia) and Nkrumah (Ghana). The Cairo preparatory meeting (1961) fixed criteria such as an independent policy, no membership of military alliances and support for liberation movements.

At Bandung (1955), 29 Asian and African states set out ten principles. It was not yet NAM, but it laid the base.

cards.h: Phase two and three: setbacks and revival
cards.b:
• 1962 China war: Nehru's idealism was hurt. India accepted Western arms and still stayed non-aligned. Lal Bahadur Shastri and Indira Gandhi took a more realist line.
  • 1971: the Indo-Soviet Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation led critics to say India was tilting. India answered that it was a response to US–China–Pakistan ties during the Bangladesh crisis.
  • 1973–74: Algiers summit and the call for a New International Economic Order.
  • 1983: the 7th summit in New Delhi. Indira Gandhi chaired NAM (1983–86). She pushed disarmament and development. Rajiv Gandhi handed over the chair at the 1986 Harare summit. India helped form the Africa Fund against apartheid.

cards.h: After the Cold War: loss of purpose?
cards.b:
When the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, there was no bloc to be non-aligned against. NAM's purpose came into doubt. Critics asked whether the movement was a 'talking shop'.

  • 1991 reforms: India sought Western capital and technology.
  • 1990s: NAM shifted its focus to development, debt, UN reform and human rights.
  • 2003 Kuala Lumpur, 2006 Havana, 2009 Sharm el-Sheikh: routine declarations.
  • 2012 Tehran: Manmohan Singh attended.
  • 2016 Margarita and 2019 Baku: Modi skipped both. India sent the Vice-President. In 2024 (Kampala, 19th summit) India was again not represented by the PM.

A key marker: Modi has not attended a NAM summit as PM, and has described foreign policy in new words.

cards.h: How NAM works, and where it split
cards.b:
• Structure: no charter or secretariat. A summit every three years, a rotating chair, a Coordinating Bureau at the UN in New York, and decisions by consensus.
  • Successes: support for decolonisation (Namibia, Zimbabwe), the long campaign against apartheid, the call for a New International Economic Order and for nuclear disarmament, and a joint voice in the UN General Assembly.
  • Splits: at Havana (1979) Fidel Castro argued that the Soviet bloc was the 'natural ally' of NAM. India and Yugoslavia opposed this and kept it autonomous. The Iran–Iraq war (1980–88) and the India–Pakistan and India–China disputes showed that NAM could not settle conflicts among its own members.
  • Size: about 120 members, with observers.

An easy way to say it: NAM was strong as a voice but weak as an institution.

Nonalignment 2.0 (2012)

A report by Sunil Khilnani, Rajiv Kumar, Srinath Raghavan, Shyam Saran and others. It said India must keep its autonomy but use it for a new world: strengthen internal capacity, build ties with all powers, and treat Asia as a priority.

S. Jaishankar, The India Way (2020)

Says non-alignment fit a bipolar world. Today India practises multi-alignment, engaging many powers on the basis of interest.

Nehru's own view

The policy was "not neutrality" but active participation in world affairs without joining blocs, in line with his book The Discovery of India (1946) and speeches in the Constituent Assembly.

Supporters say the core idea, independence of judgement, is alive in India's stance on Ukraine (no sanctions, balance with the West) and in the Quad-and-BRICS balance. Critics say that the NAM as an institution has little influence, and that India has moved close to the US on many issues.

A fair conclusion: NAM has faded, but non-alignment lives on as strategic autonomy. India's present policy is described by terms such as multi-alignment, issue-based alignment and 'strategic autonomy'.

• Ukraine: India abstained at the UN, kept buying Russian oil and also engaged Kyiv. A non-aligned style of conduct.
  • Quad plus BRICS/SCO: membership in both Western and Eurasian groupings.
  • Global South: Voice of the Global South summits since 2023 echo old NAM themes.
  • 2025–26 trade pressure: India resisted US demands on Russia, but concluded an interim framework with the US and signed new FTAs with others.
  • Gaza and Iran: India balanced ties with Israel and the Arab world and Iran.

quiz.q: The first NAM summit was held in:
Which of these was NOT among the five founders of NAM?
quiz.w: The five were Nehru, Tito, Nasser, Sukarno and Nkrumah.

quiz.q: The Bandung Conference was held in:
India hosted the NAM summit in New Delhi in:
quiz.w: The 7th summit, March 1983, chaired by Indira Gandhi.

quiz.q: Which NAM summit was attended by Manmohan Singh in 2012?
The Indo-Soviet Treaty was signed in:
Non-alignment differs from neutrality because it:
quiz.w: Non-aligned states take active positions on issues.

quiz.q: At the Havana summit of 1979, India resisted the claim that:
o: The Soviet bloc was the natural ally of NAM
quiz.w: Castro's 'natural ally' thesis was resisted by India and Yugoslavia.

quiz.q: Panchsheel was first agreed in the context of the:
quiz.w: 29 April 1954 agreement on Tibet trade and intercourse.

quiz.q: The term India now prefers for its current approach to partnerships is:
quiz.w: Jaishankar and others call it multi-alignment.
